question_text: During the approach, a crew reads on the radio altimeter the value of 650 ft. This is an indication of the true:
option_a: height of the lowest wheels with regard to the ground at any time.
option_b: height of the aircraft with regard to the ground at any time.
option_c: height of the aircraft with regard to the runway.
explanation: A radio altimeter reading represents the absolute height of the aircraft (specifically from its antennas) above the ground surface directly underneath the flight path.

question_text: Regarding Electronic Instrument System (EFIS) :1- the Navigation Display (ND) displays Flight Director Bars.2- the altimeter setting is displayed on the PFD (Primary Flight Display).3- the PFD is the main flying instrument.4- the FMA (Flight Mode Annunciator) is part of the ND.The combination regrouping all the correct statements is :
explanation: In an Electronic Flight Instrument System (EFIS), the selected altimeter setting is displayed on the PFD (Statement 2), and the PFD functions as the main piloting display (Statement 3).

question_text: The Primary Flight Display (PFD) displays information dedicated to:
option_a: piloting.
option_b: weather situation.
explanation: The Primary Flight Display (PFD) is designed to aggregate critical piloting information, including attitude, speed, altitude, vertical speed, and flight director commands.

question_text: All the last generation aircraft use flight control systems. The Flight Management System (FMS) is the most advanced system , it can be defined as a:
option_a: global 3-D Flight Management System
option_b: management system optimized in the vertical plane
option_c: management system optimized in the horizontal plane
explanation: A Flight Management System (FMS) is an integrated navigation and performance system that provides global 3-D guidance (lateral navigation, vertical navigation, and speed schedules) along the flight path.

question_text: When the altitude acquisition mode is engaged on a jet transport airplane equipped with autopilot (AP) and auto-throttle (ATS) systems the:
option_a: indicated airspeed (IAS) is maintained constant by the autopilot by means of elevator.
option_b: true airspeed (TAS) is maintained constant by the autopilot by means of elevator.
option_c: true airspeed (TAS) is maintained constant by the auto-throttle system.
option_d: indicated airspeed (IAS) is maintained constant by the auto-throttle system.
explanation: In altitude acquisition mode, the autopilot uses the elevator control loop to manage pitch and capture the preselected altitude, maintaining a constant Indicated Airspeed (IAS) in coordination with the auto-throttle.

question_text: Flight Director Information supplied by an FD computer is presented in the form of command bars on the following instrument:
option_a: ADI Attitude Display Indicator.
option_b: BDHI Bearing Distance Heading Indicator.
explanation: The Flight Director command bars (pitch and roll guides) are displayed on the Attitude Director Indicator (ADI) or the Primary Flight Display (PFD) to guide the pilot's control inputs.

question_text: The Head Up Display (HUD) is a device allowing the pilot, while still looking outside, to have:
option_a: a synthetic view of the instrument procedure.
option_b: a flying and flight path control aid.
option_d: a monitoring only during Cat III precision approaches.
explanation: A Head-Up Display (HUD) projects critical flight data, flight path vectors, and guidance symbols directly onto a transparent visor in the pilot's line of sight, serving as an advanced flight path control aid.

question_text: For capturing and keeping a preselected magnetic heading, the flight director computer takes into account:1- track deviation2- rate of track closure3- rate of change of track closure4- wind velocity given by the inertial reference unitThe combination regrouping all the correct statements is :
explanation: To capture and track a preselected heading, the flight director computer calculates the lateral track deviation (1), the rate at which the aircraft is closing on the track (2), and the acceleration rate of track closure (3).

question_text: The essential components of a flight director are :1- a computer2- an automatic pilot3- an autothrottle4- command barsThe combination of correct statements is :
explanation: The flight director system is comprised of a guidance computer (1) to calculate steering commands and the command bars (4) on the attitude indicator to display those steering cues.

question_text: The ""heading hold"" mode is selected on the flight director (FD) with a course to steer of 180°. Your aircraft holds a heading of 160°. The vertical bar of the FD:
option_a: is centered if the aircraft is on optimum path to join heading 180°
option_b: is centered if the aircraft has a starboard drift of 20°
option_c: is centered if the aircraft has a port drift of 20°
explanation: The vertical command bar of a flight director represents lateral guidance. When heading hold is active, it remains centered if the pilot is following the optimum bank angle and steering path to intercept the selected course.

question_text: Mode ""Localizer ARM"" active on Flight Director means:
option_a: System is armed for localizer approach and coupling will occur upon capturing center line
option_b: Localizer ALARM, making localizer approach not authorized
option_c: Coupling has occurred and system provides control data to capture the centerline
option_d: Localizer is armed and coupling will occur when flag warning disappears
explanation: 'Localizer ARM' mode indicates that the autopilot or flight director has been set to capture the localizer signal and will automatically transition to active tracking (coupling) when the aircraft nears the beam centerline.

question_text: An aeroplane is equipped with a Flight Director (with crosshair trend bars), heading 270°, in HDG mode (heading hold). A new heading, of 360°, is selected the vertical trend bar :
option_a: deviates to the right and will be centred as soon as you roll the aircraft to the bank angle calculated by the flight director.
option_b: deviates to the right and remains in that position until the aircraft has reached heading 360°.
option_c: disappears, the new heading selection has deactivated the HDG mode.
option_d: deviates to its right stop as long as the aeroplane is more than 10° off the new selected heading.
explanation: Selecting a new heading to the right causes the vertical steering bar to deflect right. Once the pilot banks the aircraft to the angle commanded by the flight director, the bar centers, indicating the turn is being executed correctly.

question_text: The position of a Flight Director command bars:
option_a: indicates the manoeuvers to execute, to achieve or maintain a flight situation.
option_b: repeats the ADI and HSI information
option_c: enables the measurement of deviation from a given position.
option_d: only displays information relating to radio-electric deviation.
explanation: The flight director command bars indicate the precise pitch and roll adjustments the pilot must make to fly the aircraft along the pre-programmed flight path or target profile.

question_text: On a modern aircraft, the flight director modes are displayed on the:
option_a: upper strip of the PFD (Primary Flight Display).
option_b: upper strip of the ND (Navigation Display).
option_c: upper strip of the ECAM (Electronic Centralized A/C Management).
option_d: control panel of the flight director only.
explanation: The engaged and armed modes of the flight director and autopilot are displayed in the Flight Mode Annunciator (FMA) box located on the upper strip of the Primary Flight Display (PFD).

question_text: The aim of the flight director is to provide information to the pilot:
option_a: allowing him to return to a desired path in an optimal way.
option_b: about his position with regard to a radioelectric axis.
option_c: allowing him to return to a desired path according to a 45° intercept angle.
option_d: allowing him to return to a desired path according to a 30° intercept angle.
explanation: The primary aim of the flight director is to calculate and display real-time steering commands that allow the pilot to capture and maintain a desired flight path or target profile optimally.

question_text: (For this question use annex 022-9768A)An aircraft is under guidance mode following a VOR radial. From the ADI and HSI information represented in the enclosed annex, it is possible to deduce that the aircraft is :
option_a: experiencing a leftside wind.
option_b: located to the leftside of the selected radial.
option_c: located to the rightside of the selected radial.
explanation: By comparing the heading, track, and drift indications on the ADI and HSI, the offset shows the aircraft is crabbed to the right to maintain the radial, indicating a wind component coming from the left.

question_text: The flight director indicates the :
option_a: optimum instantaneous path to reach selected radial.
option_b: optimum path at the moment it is entered to reach a selected radial.
option_c: path permitting reaching a selected radial in minimum time.
option_d: path permitting reaching a selected radial over a minimum distance.
explanation: The flight director continuously computes and displays the optimum instantaneous steering commands required to intercept and track a selected radial or flight path.

question_text: For this question use annex (022-10179A)Four scenarios of VOR axis interception are represented in the appended annex. The one corresponding to the optimal interception path calculated by a flight director is number :
explanation: Scenario 2 illustrates the optimal, asymptotic interception path calculated by the flight director, which prevents overshooting the target VOR radial centerline.

question_text: The command bars of a flight director are generally represented on an:
option_a: ADI (Attitude Director Indicator)
option_b: HSI (Horizontal Situation Indicator)
explanation: Flight director command bars are displayed on the Attitude Director Indicator (ADI), or its electronic equivalent (the PFD), superimposing pitch and roll commands over the attitude display.

question_text: (For this question use annex 022-10217A)After having programmed your flight director, you see that the indications of your ADI (Attitude Director Indicator) are as represented in diagram N°1 of the appended annex. On this instrument, the command bars indicate that you must bank your airplane to the left and :
option_a: increase the flight attitude until the command bars recentre on the symbolic airplane.
option_b: decrease the flight attitude until the command bars recentre on the symbolic airplane.
option_c: increase the flight attitude until the command bars recentre on the horizon.
option_d: decrease the flight attitude until the command bars recentre on the horizon.
explanation: In Diagram 1, the pitch bar is above the symbolic airplane. To follow this command, the pilot must pull back to pitch up (increase flight attitude) until the symbolic airplane nose aligns with the pitch bar.

question_text: (For this question use annex 022-11232A)After having programmed your flight director, you see that the indications of your ADI (Attitude Director indicator) are as represented in diagram N°1 of the appended annex. On this instrument, the command bars indicate that you must :
option_a: increase the flight attitude and bank your airplane to the left until the command bars recentre on the symbolic aeroplane.
option_b: increase the flight attitude and bank your aeroplane to the right until the command bars recentre on the symbolic aeroplane.
option_c: decrease the flight attitude and bank your airplane to the left until the command bars recentre on the symbolic aeroplane.
option_d: decrease the flight attitude and bank your airplane to the right until the command bars recentre on the symbolic aeroplane.
explanation: According to the crosshair command bars in the diagram, the horizontal bar is high (requiring a pitch-up) and the vertical bar is to the left (requiring a left bank). The pilot must combine these inputs until the command bars recenter on the aircraft symbol.

question_text: The synchronization of the autopilot control channel system :1- enables the prevention of jerks during disengagement 2- enables the cancellation of rudder control signals3- enables the prevention of jerks during engagement4- functions in the heading, navigation, approach modesThe combination regrouping all the correct statements is:
explanation: The synchronization system aligns the autopilot servo actuators with the current flight control position prior to engagement, preventing sudden control inputs (jerks) when engaging the autopilot (3) across various flight modes (4).

question_text: (For this question use annex 022-3880A)The block diagram of an auto-pilot is shown in the annex.For each control channel (pitch, roll and yaw) the piloting law is the relationship between the deflection of the control surface commanded by the computer (BETA c) and the:
option_a: offset EPSILON at the computer input.
option_b: pilot command E.
option_d: real deflection of the control surface (BETA control surface feedback).
explanation: The piloting law of an autopilot channel determines the commanded control surface deflection (BETA c) as a function of the error offset (EPSILON) detected at the input of the flight control computer.

question_text: Landing shall be considered as having been carried out automatically when the autopilot and the auto-throttle of an aircraft are disengaged by flight crew :
option_a: during ground roll.
option_b: during the flare.
explanation: A landing is considered fully automatic if the autopilot and auto-throttle remain engaged to guide the aircraft through touchdown and flare, and are only disengaged by the crew during the rollout on the runway.

question_text: A pilot has to carry out a single-pilot IFR flight on a light twin-engined aircraft for cargo transport. The purpose of the automatic pilot is at least to hold the:
option_a: heading and to hold the altitude
option_b: heading
option_d: heading, to hold the altitude and to have a radio axis tracking function
explanation: To meet regulatory requirements for single-pilot IFR operations, the autopilot must at least be capable of stabilizing the flight path by holding a selected heading and maintaining a selected altitude.

question_text: An automatic landing is carried out when the automatic pilot :
option_a: and the autothrottle ensure a correct final approach, at least up to ground roll
option_b: ensures a correct final approach, at least up to ground roll while the human pilot controls the power
option_c: and the autothrottle ensure a correct final approach, at least up to flare-out
option_d: and the autothrottle ensure a correct final approach, at least up to flare-out while the human pilot controls the power
explanation: An automatic landing requires that both the autopilot (for flight path tracking) and the auto-throttle (for speed management) control the aircraft down through flare and touchdown to the ground roll.

question_text: A closed loop control system in which a small power input controls a much larger power output in a strictly proportionate manner is known as :
option_a: a servomechanism.
option_b: an amplifier.
explanation: A servomechanism is a closed-loop control system that uses feedback to control a mechanical position, speed, or other parameter, amplifying a small input signal into a proportionate high-power output.

question_text: The interception of a localizer beam by the autopilot takes place :
option_a: at a constant heading
option_b: at a constant magnetic course
option_c: according to an interception versus radio deviation law
option_d: according to an interception versus range and angular
explanation: The autopilot intercept loop calculates the intercept path and roll commands as a function of the radio deviation (lateral angular distance) from the localizer beam centerline.

question_text: The Altitude Select System:
option_a: Is annunciated by light and/or sound when airplane is approaching selected altitude
option_b: Illuminates a light when selected altitude is attained
option_c: Engages autopilot Auto Trim at selected altitude
option_d: Disengages autopilot Auto Trim at selected altitude
explanation: The altitude alerter or select system generates visual and/or aural warnings to notify the flight crew when the aircraft is approaching or deviating from a preselected altitude.

question_text: On an autopilot coupled approach, GO AROUND mode is engaged:
option_a: by the pilot pushing a button located on the throttles.
option_b: by the pilot selecting G.A. mode on the thrust computer control panel.
option_c: automatically in case of an autopilot or flight director alarm.
option_d: if the aircraft reaches the decision height selected on the radio altimeter at a higher speed than the one selected.
explanation: Go-around (GA) mode on a coupled approach is engaged by the pilot pushing the takeoff/go-around (TO/GA) switch or button located directly on the thrust levers (throttles).

question_text: When being engaged, and without selecting a particular mode, an automatic pilot enables :
option_a: aeroplane stabilisation with attitude hold or maintaining vertical speed and possibly automatic trim.
option_b: aeroplane piloting and guidance functions.
option_c: a constant speed on track, wings horizontal.
option_d: all aeroplane piloting and guidance functions except maintaining radio-navigation course lines.
explanation: When the autopilot is engaged without selecting a flight director guidance mode, it defaults to basic stabilization, maintaining the current pitch/roll attitude or vertical speed, and engages auto-trim.

question_text: An automatic pilot is a system which can ensure the functions of:
option_a: piloting and guidance of an aircraft in both the horizontal and vertical planes.
option_b: piloting only.
option_d: piloting from take-off to landing without any action from the human pilot.
explanation: An autopilot is designed to perform both basic stabilization (piloting) and path tracking (guidance) of the aircraft in the pitch, roll, and yaw axes.

question_text: When the auto-pilot is engaged, the role of the automatic trim is to:
option_a: relieve the A.P. servo motor and return the aircraft in-trim at A.P. disconnect
option_b: relieve the pressure on the control column and return, the aircraft in-trim at A.P. disconnect
option_c: react to altitude changes in Altitude Hold mode
explanation: The auto-trim system continuously adjusts the stabilizer trim to relieve aerodynamic loads on the autopilot pitch servo motor. This ensures the aircraft remains in a trimmed state when the autopilot is disconnected.

question_text: The command functions of an autopilot include, among others, the holding of :1- vertical speed2- altitude3- attitude4- bank5- headingThe combination which regroups all of the correct statements is :
explanation: Autopilot command functions include holding vertical speed (Statement 1), altitude (Statement 2), and heading (Statement 5), which matches the '2001-02-05' option (statements 1, 2, and 5).

question_text: In an auto-pilot slaved powered control circuit, the system which ensures synchronisation :
option_a: can itself, when it fails, prevent the automatic pilot from being engaged.
option_b: intervenes only when the automatic pilot has been engaged.
option_c: prevents uncommanded surface deflection when the automatic pilot is disengaged.
option_d: is inhibited when the automatic pilot is engaged.
explanation: Autopilot engagement logic checks that the synchronization circuit is functioning. If the synchronization system fails, the autopilot will refuse to engage to prevent unsafe control movements.

question_text: The control law of a transport airplane autopilot control channel may be defined as the relationship between the :
option_a: computer input deviation data and the output control deflection signals.
option_b: computer input deviation data and the signals received by the servoactuators.
option_c: input and output signals at the amplifier level respectively control deviation data and control deflection signals.
option_d: crew inputs to the computer and the detector responses (returned to the airplane).
explanation: The control law defines the mathematical relationship between the error input signals (deviation from the target heading, altitude, etc.) and the computed output deflection commands sent to the control surface servos.

question_text: In a transport airplane, an autopilot comprises, in addition to the mode display devices, the following fundamental elements :1- Airflow valve2- Sensors3- Comparators4- Computers5- Amplifiers6- Servo-actuatorsThe combination regrouping all the correct statements is:
explanation: A standard autopilot feedback loop includes sensors (2) to detect attitude, comparators (3) to calculate deviations, flight computers (4) to run control laws, amplifiers (5) to increase signal strength, and servo-actuators (6) to move the surfaces.

question_text: The correction of the control surface deflection made by the automatic pilot calculator in order to stabilize the longitudinal attitude will be all the more significant as the :1- difference between the reference attitude and the instantaneous attitude is high.2- rate of change of the difference between the reference attitude and the instantaneous attitude is high.3- temperature is low.4- pressure altitude is high.The combination regrouping all the correct statements is:
explanation: Pitch stabilization correction commands are proportional to the size of the attitude error (1) and the rate at which the attitude is changing (2).

question_text: The correction of the control surface deflection made by the auto-pilot calculator in order to keep a given altitude will be all the more significant when the :1- difference between the attitude necessary to keep the given or reference altitude and the instantaneous attitude is high.2 - variation speed of the difference between the attitude necessary to maintain the altitude and the instantaneous attitude is high.3 - difference between the altitude of reference and the instantaneous altitude is high.4 - variation speed of the difference between the reference altitude and the instantaneous altitude is high.The combination regrouping the correct statements is:
option_b: 1 and 2.
explanation: To maintain a selected altitude, the autopilot uses proportional-derivative loops, requiring inputs for pitch deviation (1), pitch rate (2), altitude error (3), and vertical speed/altitude rate (4).

question_text: When only one autopilot is used for climbing, cruising and approach, the system is considered:
option_a: ""fail soft"" or with minimized failure effect.
option_b: ""fail passive"" or without failure effect but with disconnection.
option_c: ""fail survival"" or without failure effect with function always ensured.
option_d: ""fail safe"" with failure effect without disconnection.
explanation: A single autopilot configuration is designed to be 'fail-soft'. In the event of a malfunction, it will disconnect cleanly without causing dangerous transient maneuvers, requiring the pilot to immediately take manual control.

question_text: In automatic landing mode, when the 2 autopilots are used, the system is considered:
option_a: ""fail survival"" or without failure effect with function always ensured.
option_b: ""fail soft"" or with minimized failure effect.
option_c: ""fail passive"" or without failure effect but with disconnection.
option_d: ""fail hard"" or with failure effect and disconnection.
explanation: During automatic landing, two or more autopilots operate in parallel. If one autopilot fails, the remaining unit(s) seamlessly maintain control (fail-operational/fail-survival) to ensure the landing is completed safely.

question_text: In automatic landing mode, in case of failure of one of the two autopilots, the system is considered:
option_a: ""fail passive"" or without failure effect but with disconnection.
option_b: ""fail survival"" or without failure effect with function always ensured.
option_c: ""fail hard"" or without failure effect and disconnection.
explanation: In a standard dual-channel autoland system, a failure of one autopilot drops the redundancy level from fail-operational to fail-passive, meaning a subsequent failure will result in automatic disengagement, requiring manual takeover.

question_text: During an automatic landing, from a height of about 50 ft the:
option_a: autopilot maintains a vertical speed depending on the radio altimeter height.
option_b: glideslope mode is disconnected and the airplane continues its descent until landing.
option_c: autopilot maintains an angle of attack depending on the radio altimeter height.
option_d: Loc and Glideslope modes are disconnected and the airplane carries on its descent until landing.
explanation: During automatic landing, the flare phase begins at approximately 50 feet. The autopilot disconnects Glideslope mode and executes a programmed pitch-up maneuver to reduce vertical speed as a function of the decreasing radio altitude.

question_text: In a selected axis capture mode, the autopilot gives a bank attitude input :
option_a: proportional to the deviation between the selected heading and the current heading but not exceeding a given value.
option_b: of a fixed value equal to 27°.
option_c: of a fixed value equal to 20°.
option_d: proportional to the aircraft true airspeed but not exceeding a given value.
explanation: During intercept turns, the autopilot commands a bank angle proportional to the heading error, limited to a maximum angle (usually 25° or 30°) to maintain passenger comfort and structural safety.

question_text: An automatic landing system which can keep on operating without deterioration of its performances following the failure of one of the autopilots is called ""FAIL...:
option_a: ""OPERATIONAL""
option_b: ""PASSIVE""
explanation: A system is classified as 'fail-operational' (or fail-operational/fail-survival) if it can continue to perform its function normally without degradation in performance after a single component failure.

question_text: An automatic landing system necessitating that the landing be continued manually in the case of a system failure during an automatic approach is called ""FAIL....""
option_a: ""PASSIVE""
option_b: ""OPERATIONAL""
explanation: A system is 'fail-passive' if, in the event of a failure, there is no significant out-of-trim condition or deviation from the flight path, but the system disconnects, requiring the pilot to take manual control.

question_text: A semi-automatic landing system disconnects itself automatically:
option_a: at approximately 100 ft.
option_b: at the decision height.
explanation: In a semi-automatic landing system, the autopilot provides guidance down the approach path but automatically disconnects at a designated low altitude (e.g., 100 ft), requiring the pilot to execute the flare and touchdown manually.

question_text: A landing is performed automatically when the autopilot and auto-throttle ensure good performance from the final approach :
option_a: during the landing roll and sometimes until the aircraft comes to a complete stop.
option_b: until reaching 100 ft, height at which point the autopilot is automatically disconnected.
explanation: A fully automatic landing includes the final approach, flare, touchdown, and runway rollout control, remaining engaged through the landing roll until disengaged by the pilot.

question_text: When an aircraft, operating in the VOR coupled mode, approaches the ""cone of confusion"" over a VOR station, the roll channel of the autopilot :
option_a: temporarily switches over to the heading mode.
option_b: is damped by a trim input signal from the lateral trim system.
option_c: remains always coupled to the selected VOR radial.
explanation: When passing directly over a VOR station, the signals fluctuate rapidly (the cone of confusion). The autopilot filters this out by temporarily switching from VOR tracking to Heading Hold mode until stable radial signals are re-acquired.

question_text: The autopilot basic modes include, among other things, the following functions :1- pitch attitude hold 2- pressure altitude hold3- horizontal wing hold4- heading hold The combination regrouping all the correct statements is :
explanation: The basic modes of an autopilot stabilize and control the aircraft's attitude (pitch, roll, and yaw) about its center of gravity.

question_text: During a Category II automatic approach, the height information is supplied by the :
option_a: radio altimeter.
option_b: GPS (Global Positioning System).
explanation: Category II and III precision approaches require highly accurate height-above-ground information during the final stages of the approach, which is supplied exclusively by the radio altimeter.

question_text: A pilot engages the control wheel steering (CWS) of a conventional autopilot and carries out a manoeuvre in roll. When the control wheel is released, the autopilot will :
option_a: maintain the flight attitude obtained at that moment.
option_b: roll wings level and maintain the heading obtained at that moment.
option_c: maintain the track and the flight attitude obtained at that moment.
option_d: restore the flight attitude and the rate of turn selected on the autopilot control display unit.
explanation: In Control Wheel Steering (CWS) mode, the pilot can manually fly the aircraft using normal control inputs. When the controls are released, the autopilot holds the current pitch and bank attitude achieved at that instant.

question_text: The functions of an autopilot (basic modes) consist of :
option_a: stabilizing and monitoring the movement around the airplane centre of gravity.
option_b: monitoring the movement of the airplane centre of gravity.
option_d: stabilizing and monitoring the movement around the airplane aerodynamic centre.
explanation: The basic modes of an autopilot stabilize and control the aircraft's attitude (pitch, roll, and yaw) about its center of gravity.

question_text: From a flight mechanics point of view, the ""guidance"" functions of a transport airplane autopilot consist in:
option_a: monitoring the movements of the centre of gravity in the three dimensions of space (path).
option_b: stabilizing and monitoring the movements around the centre of gravity.
option_c: monitoring the movements of the aerodynamic centre in the three dimensions of space (path).
option_d: stabilizing and monitoring the movements around the aerodynamic centre.
explanation: The guidance functions of an autopilot track the aircraft's center of gravity along a designated 3-dimensional trajectory (flight path) through space using navigation references.

question_text: An autopilot capable of holding at least altitude and heading mode is compulsory:
option_a: for IFR or night flights with only one pilot.
option_b: on multipilot airplanes.
option_c: for VFR and IFR flights with only one pilot.
explanation: Under aviation regulations, a single-pilot IFR or night flight in commercial operations requires a functioning autopilot equipped with at least heading and altitude hold modes.

question_text: Among the following functions of an autopilot, those related to the airplane stabilization are:1- pitch attitude holding2- horizontal wing holding3- displayed heading or inertial track holding4- indicated airspeed or Mach number holding5- yaw damping6- VOR axis holdingThe combination regrouping all the correct statements is:
explanation: Stabilization involves controlling attitude and rotation rates about the aircraft axes, which includes pitch attitude hold (1), wings level hold (2), and yaw damping (5).

question_text: Among the following functions of an autopilot, those related to the airplane guidance are:1- pitch attitude holding2- horizontal wing holding3- indicated airspeed or Mach number holding4- altitude holding5- VOR axis holding6- yaw dampingThe combination regrouping all the correct statements is:
explanation: Guidance involves controlling the flight path relative to an external reference, which includes tracking airspeed/Mach schedules (3), maintaining a pressure altitude (4), and tracking VOR radials (5).

question_text: When using the autopilot, the function of the pitch channel automatic trim is to:1- cancel the hinge moment of the elevator2- ease as much as possible the load of the servo-actuator 3- restore to the pilot a correctly trimmed airplane during the autopilot disengagement The combination regrouping all the correct statements is:
explanation: Auto-trim cancels the elevator hinge moments (1), reduces load on the AP pitch servo actuator (2), and ensures the aircraft is properly trimmed when the autopilot is disconnected (3).

question_text: A landing will be considered to be performed in the SEMI-AUTOMATIC mode when:1- the autopilot maintains the airplane on the ILS beam until the decision height is reached then is disengaged automatically.2- the autothrottle maintains a constant speed until the decision height is reached then is disengaged automatically.3- the autopilot maintains the airplane on the ILS beam until the flare.4- the autothrottle decreases the thrust when the height is approximately 30 ft.5- the flare and the ground roll are performed automatically.The combination regrouping all the correct statements is:
option_a: 1 and 2.
explanation: A landing is semi-automatic if the autopilot and autothrottle guide the aircraft down to decision height (Statements 1 and 2), at which point the pilot disconnects them and completes the landing manually.

question_text: A landing will be considered to be performed in the AUTOMATIC mode when:1- the autopilot maintains the airplane on the ILS beam until the decision height is reached then is disengaged automatically.2- the autothrottle maintains a constant speed until the decision height is reached then is disengaged automatically.3- the autopilot maintains the airplane on the ILS beam until the flare.4- the autothrottle decreases the thrust when the height is approximately 30 ft.5- the flare and the ground roll are performed automatically.The combination regrouping all the correct statements is:
option_b: 1 and 2.
explanation: An automatic landing is characterized by the autopilot tracking the ILS beam to the flare (3), the autothrottle automatically retarding thrust at 30 feet (4), and both systems performing the flare and ground rollout automatically (5).

question_text: When an automatic landing is interrupted by a go-around :1- the autothrottle reacts immediately upon the pilot action on the TO/GA (Take-off/Go-around) switch in order to recover the maximum thrust2- the autopilot monitors the climb and the rotation of the airplane3- the autopilot retracts the landing gear and reduces the flap deflection in order to reduce the drag4- the pilot performs the climb and the rotation of the airplane5- the pilot retracts the landing gear and reduces the flap deflection in order to reduce the dragThe combination regrouping all the correct statements is:
explanation: During a go-around, the autothrottle commands go-around thrust when the TO/GA switch is pushed (1), the autopilot flies the pitch rotation and climb profiles (2), and the pilot manages drag by retracting the landing gear and flaps (5).

question_text: The calibrated airspeed (CAS) or Mach holding mode is carried out by:1- the autopilot pitch channel in the climb mode at a constant calibrated airspeed (CAS) or Mach number2- the autothrottles in the climb mode at a constant calibrated airspeed (CAS) or Mach number3- the autopilot pitch channel in the altitude or glide path holding mode4- the autothrottles in the altitude or glide path holding modeThe combination regrouping all the correct statements is:
option_a: 1 and 4.
option_b: 2 and 4.
explanation: Airspeed or Mach hold can be performed by the autopilot pitch channel controlling pitch (1) during climbs/descents, or by the autothrottles controlling engine thrust (4) during level flight.

question_text: The engagement of an autopilot is not possible when:1- there is a fault in the electrical power supply2- the controlled-turn knob is not set to centre-off3- there is a synchronization fault in the pitch channel4- there is a fault in the attitude reference unitThe combination regrouping all the correct statements is:
explanation: Autopilot engagement is prohibited if there is a power supply failure (1), the turn knob is not centered (2), pitch channel synchronization is out of limit (3), or the attitude reference unit has a fault (4).

question_text: An autopilot is selected ""ON"" in mode ""altitude hold,"" the pilot alters the barometric pressure set on the sub-scale of his altimeter the:
option_a: aircraft will remain at the same altitude, the autopilot takes its pressure information from the static source
option_b: aircraft will remain at the same altitude, the autopilot takes its pressure information from the altimeter corrected to standard pressure, 1013.25 hPa
option_c: aircraft will climb or descend in the sense of the change, the autopilot takes its pressure information from the altimeter
explanation: If the pilot adjusts the altimeter's barometric subscale while in altitude hold, the altimeter's reported altitude shifts. The autopilot, referencing this altimeter data, will climb or descend to match the new pressure reference.

question_text: The computers of the electrical flight controls system comply with programs defined by attitude control laws such as :1- on the longitudinal axis, the law may combine the load factor and the changes in the pitch rate as control data sources2- the trimming is automatic and ensures neutral stability3- the protections apply to pitch and bank attitudes depending on the speed4- these laws do not apply to the whole flight envelope The combination regrouping all the correct statements is:
explanation: Electrical Flight Control Systems (EFCS) use control laws combining load factor and pitch rate (1), provide automatic pitch trimming (2), and offer flight envelope protections for pitch and bank (3).

question_text: The yaw damper, which suppresses Dutch roll:
option_a: controls the rudder, with the angular rate about the vertical axis as the input signal.
option_b: controls the ailerons, with Mach Number as the input signal.
option_c: controls the rudder, with Mach Number as the input signal.
option_d: controls the ailerons, with the angular rate about the vertical axis as the input signal.
explanation: The yaw damper detects yaw rate (angular velocity about the vertical axis) using a rate gyro and sends corrective commands directly to the rudder actuator to damp out Dutch roll.

question_text: The yaw damper indicator supplies the pilot with information regarding the:
option_a: yaw damper action on the rudder
option_b: rudder displacement by the rudder pedals
option_c: yaw damper action only on the ground
explanation: The yaw damper indicator displays the instantaneous surface deflection angle applied to the rudder by the yaw damper system.

question_text: The automatic trim is a component of the autopilot pitch channel. Its function is to:
option_a: transfer a stabilized aeroplane to the pilot during autopilot disengagement.
option_b: reset the attitude, after engaging (the autopilot).
option_c: set the attitude to an instantaneous value before engaging the autopilot.
option_d: automatically disengage the autopilot in the case of an excessive pitch up.
explanation: Auto-trim continuously nulls the loads on the autopilot pitch servos, ensuring the aircraft is properly trimmed and stable when control is transferred back to the pilot upon AP disconnect.

question_text: Which one of the following statements is true with regard to the operation of a Mach trim system :
option_a: It only operates above a pre-determined Mach number.
option_b: It operates to counteract the larger than normal forward movements of the wing centre of pressure at high subsonic airspeeds.
option_c: It only operates when the autopilot is engaged.
option_d: It operates over the full aircraft speed range.
explanation: Mach trim is designed to counter 'Mach tuck' (the nose-down pitching moment caused by the aft movement of the center of pressure at high speeds). It is programmed to operate automatically only above a specific high Mach number (typically M 0.6 or M 0.7).

question_text: In the automatic trim control system of an autopilot, automatic trimming is normally effected about the :
option_a: pitch axis only.
option_b: roll and yaw axes only.
explanation: In most transport aircraft autopilot systems, automatic trim is primary to the pitch axis (via the stabilizer) to relieve pitch servo loads.

question_text: Mach Trim is a device to compensate for :
option_a: backing of the aerodynamic center at high Mach numbers by moving the elevator to nose-up
option_b: the effects of fuel transfer between the main tanks and the tank located in the horizontal tail
option_c: the effects of temperature variation during a climb or descent at constant Mach
option_d: weight reduction resulting from fuel consumption during the cruise
explanation: Mach trim corrects for the rearward shift of the wing's center of pressure (aerodynamic center) at high Mach numbers by automatically commanding a small nose-up elevator deflection.

question_text: The purpose of Auto Trim function in autopilot is to :
option_a: control elevator trim tab in order to relieve elevator load
option_b: help Auto Pilot compensate for crosswind influence
option_c: tell the pilot when elevator trimming is required
option_d: trim throttles to obtain smooth engine power variation
explanation: The primary purpose of the auto-trim system is to drive the pitch trim (stabilizer or trim tab) to relieve the steady aerodynamic force on the elevator servos.

question_text: The purpose of an airplane automatic trim system is to trim out the hinge moment of the :
option_a: elevator(s)
option_b: rudder(s)
explanation: The automatic trim system of the autopilot is designed to eliminate the aerodynamic hinge moments acting on the elevators, ensuring a trimmed pitch state.

question_text: The purpose of the automatic trim is to:1- reduce to zero the hinge moment of the entire control surface in order to relieve the load on the servo-actuator2- ensure the aeroplane is properly trimmed when the autopilot is disengaged3- maintain the same stability/manoeuverablity trade-off within the whole flight envelopeThe combination regrouping all the correct statements is:
explanation: Auto trim reduces the servo load to zero (1), ensures the aircraft is trimmed on AP disconnect (2), and maintains consistent handling qualities throughout the flight envelope (3).

question_text: A Full Authority Digital Engine Control (FADEC) has the following functions :1- flow regulation (fuel, decelerations and accelerations monitoring)2- automatic starting sequence 3- transmissions of engine data to the pilot's instruments4- thrust management and protection of operation limits 5- monitoring of the thrust reversersThe combination regrouping all the correct statements is:
explanation: A FADEC system is a highly integrated engine control computer managing fuel flow (1), starting sequences (2), instrument outputs (3), operational limits and protections (4), and thrust reversers (5).

question_text: The Engine Pressure Ratio (EPR) is computed by :
option_a: dividing turbine discharge pressure by compressor inlet pressure.
option_b: dividing compressor discharge pressure by turbine discharge pressure.
option_c: multiplying compressor inlet pressure by turbine discharge pressure.
option_d: multiplying compressor discharge pressure by turbine inlet pressure.
explanation: Engine Pressure Ratio (EPR) is the ratio of the total pressure at the turbine exhaust (discharge pressure) to the total pressure at the compressor inlet.

question_text: An aeroplane is in steady climb. The autothrottle maintains a constant calibrated airspeed. If the total temperature remains constant, the Mach number :
option_a: increases.
option_b: decreases.
option_d: decreases if the static temperature is lower than the standard temperature.
explanation: If temperature remains constant during a climb, the speed of sound remains constant. Since air density decreases, the TAS must increase to maintain a constant CAS, which causes the Mach number (TAS/LSS) to increase.

question_text: The two main sources of information used to calculate turbojet thrust are the:
option_a: fan rotation speed (or N1) or the EPR (Engine Pressure Ratio).
option_b: high pressure turbine rotation speed or the EPR (Engine Pressure Ratio).
option_c: fan rotation speed (or N1) or the total pressure at the high pressure compressor outlet.
option_d: fan rotation speed (or N1) or the total pressure at the low pressure turbine outlet.
explanation: The two primary cockpit indications of engine thrust on modern turbofans are the low-pressure rotor speed (N1) or the Engine Pressure Ratio (EPR).

question_text: An airplane is in steady cruise at flight level 290. The autothrottle maintains a constant Mach number. If the total temperature increases, the calibrated airspeed:
option_a: remains constant.
option_b: increases.
option_d: increases if the static temperature is higher than the standard temperature, decreases if lower.
explanation: Since Mach number is a function of the ratio of dynamic pressure to static pressure, maintaining a constant Mach number at a constant pressure altitude (constant static pressure) means the dynamic pressure remains constant, and therefore CAS remains constant regardless of temperature changes.

question_text: An airplane is in steady cruise at flight level 290. The autothrottle maintains a constant Mach number. If the total temperature decreases, the calibrated airspeed:
option_a: remains constant.
option_b: increases.
option_d: decreases if the outside temperature is lower than the standard temperature, increases if higher.
explanation: At a constant flight level, maintaining a constant Mach number keeps the ratio of dynamic to static pressure constant. Since static pressure is constant, the dynamic pressure is also constant, keeping CAS constant.

question_text: An airplane is in steady descent. The autothrottle maintains a constant Mach number. If the total temperature remains constant, the calibrated airspeed:
option_a: increases.
option_b: decreases.
option_d: decreases if the static temperature is lower than the standard temperature, increases if above.
explanation: In descent, static pressure increases. For a constant Mach number, the dynamic pressure (which is proportional to Mach squared times static pressure) must increase. This results in an increasing Calibrated Airspeed (CAS).

question_text: An aeroplane is in steady cruise at flight level 270. The autothrottle maintains a constant calibrated airspeed. If the total temperature increases, the Mach number :
option_a: remains constant.
option_b: increases.
option_d: decreases if the outside temperature is higher than the standard temperature, increases if lower.
explanation: At a constant pressure altitude, holding a constant CAS keeps the dynamic pressure constant. Since the static pressure is also constant, the ratio of dynamic to static pressure is unchanged, meaning the Mach number remains constant.

question_text: An aeroplane is in steady cruise at flight level 270. The autothrottle maintains a constant calibrated airspeed. If the total temperature decreases, the Mach number :
option_a: remains constant.
option_b: increases.
option_d: increases if the outside temperature is higher than the standard temperature, decreases if lower.
explanation: At a constant flight level, static pressure is fixed. Maintaining a constant CAS means dynamic pressure is fixed. Since Mach is a function of the ratio of dynamic to static pressure, the Mach number remains constant.

question_text: An aeroplane is in a steady climb. The autothrottle maintains a constant Mach number. If the total temperature remains constant, the calibrated airspeed :
option_a: decreases.
option_b: increases.
option_d: decreases if the static temperature is lower than the standard temperature, increases if higher.
explanation: During a climb, static pressure decreases. To maintain a constant Mach number, the dynamic pressure must also decrease, which results in a decreasing Calibrated Airspeed (CAS).

question_text: An aeroplane is in steady descent. The autothrottle maintains a constant calibrated airspeed. If the total temperature remains constant, the Mach number :
option_a: decreases.
option_b: increases.
option_d: increases if the static temperature is lower than the standard temperature, decreases if higher.
explanation: During descent, static pressure increases. For a constant CAS (constant dynamic pressure), the ratio of dynamic to static pressure decreases, causing the Mach number to decrease.

question_text: The autothrottle :1- enable to catch and to maintain the N1 RPM2- enable to catch and to maintain the N2 RPM3- enable to catch and to maintain an airplane indicated airspeed (IAS)4- is always engaged automatically at the same time as the autopilotThe combination regrouping all the correct statements is:
option_a: 1 and 3
option_b: 2 and 3
explanation: The autothrottle system manages the engines to maintain either a target N1 RPM (1) or a targeted indicated airspeed/Mach (3). It does not maintain N2 RPM directly.

question_text: The purpose of Auto Throttle is:
option_a: to maintain constant engine power or airplane speed
option_b: automatic shut down of one engine at too high temperature
option_c: to deactivate manual throttles and transfer engine control to Auto Pilot
explanation: The autothrottle automatically modulates engine thrust levers to maintain a selected engine power limit (such as N1 or EPR) or a target flight speed (IAS/Mach).

question_text: In order to know in which mode the autothrottles are engaged, the crew will check the :
option_a: PFD (Primary Flight Display)
option_b: ND (Navigation Display).
explanation: Autothrottle engagement modes (such as THRUST, SPEED, or RETARD) are annunciated on the Flight Mode Annunciator (FMA) section at the top of the Primary Flight Display (PFD).

question_text: The automatic power control system (autothrottle) of a transport airplane has the following mode(s) :1- capture and holding of speeds2- capture and holding of Mach number3- capture and holding of flight angle of attack4- capture and holding of N1 or EPR (Engine Power Ratio)5- capture and holding of flight pathsThe combination regrouping all the correct statements is :
explanation: The autothrottle control loops include speed hold (1), Mach hold (2), and engine power limit hold (N1 or EPR) (4).

question_text: Alarms are standardised and follow a code of colours. Those requiring action but not immediately, are signalled by the colour:
option_a: amber
option_b: red
explanation: Under EASA standards, cockpit warning lights are color-coded: red indicates a warning requiring immediate crew action, while amber signifies a caution requiring crew awareness and subsequent action, but not immediately.

question_text: A transport airplane has to be equipped with an altitude warning device. This system will warn the crew about :1 - getting close to the preselected altitude, during both climb and descent.2 - getting close to the preselected altitude, during climb only.3 - the loss of altitude during take-off or missed approach.4 - a wrong landing configuration.5 - a variation higher or lower than a preselected altitude.The combination regrouping the correct statements is:
explanation: The altitude alerting system is required to warn the crew when approaching a preselected altitude during both climb and descent (1), and in the event of a deviation above or below that preselected altitude (5).

question_text: An ""altitude warning system"" must at least warn the crew :1- when approaching the pre-selected altitude2- when the airplane is approaching the ground too fast3- in case of a given deviation above or below the pre-selected altitude (at least by an aural warning)4- in case of excessive vertical speed5- when approaching the ground with the gear retractedThe combination regrouping all the correct statements is :
explanation: The altitude alert system is designed specifically to alert the crew when approaching a preselected altitude (1) and when departing from it (3). Ground proximity warnings are handled by the separate GPWS system.

question_text: The purpose of the altitude alert system is to generate a visual and aural warning to the pilot when the:
option_a: airplane altitude differs from a selected altitude.
option_b: airplane altitude is equal to the decision altitude.
option_c: proximity to the ground becomes dangerous.
option_d: altimeter setting differs from the standard setting above the transition altitude.
explanation: The primary function of the altitude alert system is to warn the pilot with visual and aural cues if the aircraft deviates from the preselected target altitude.

question_text: The GPWS calculator receives the following signals :1 - vertical speed2 - radio altimeter height3 - pressure altitude4 - glidepath deviation 5 - gear and flaps position6 - angle of attackThe combination regrouping all the correct statements is :
explanation: To calculate ground proximity threats, a standard GPWS computer receives vertical speed (1), radio altimeter height (2), ILS glideslope deviation (4), and landing configuration status like gear/flaps (5).

question_text: The GPWS calculator is able to operate in the following modes :1- excessive descent rate 2- excessive rate of terrain closure3- excessive angle of attack4- too high descent attitude 5- loss of altitude after take-off6- abnormal gear/flaps configuration7- excessive glidepath deviationThe combination regrouping all the correct statements is:
explanation: GPWS operates in 5 basic modes: excessive descent rate (1), excessive terrain closure rate (2), altitude loss after take-off/go-around (5), unsafe landing gear/flap configuration (6), and excessive glideslope deviation (7).

question_text: The GPWS (Ground Proximity Warning System) is active for a height range from:
option_a: 50 ft to 2 500 ft measured by the radio altimeter.
option_b: 0 ft to 2 500 ft measured by the radio altimeter.
option_c: 0 ft to 5 000 ft measured by the radio altimeter.
option_d: 50 ft to 5 000 ft measured by the radio altimeter.
explanation: Conventional Ground Proximity Warning Systems are designed to generate terrain alerts when the aircraft is between 50 and 2,500 feet above the ground, using the radio altimeter to measure absolute clearance.

question_text: The Ground Proximity Warning System (GPWS) generates the following sound signal or signals when the aircraft is sinking after a take-off or a go-around :
option_a: DON'T SINK repetitive only
option_b: WHOOP WHOOP PULL UP repetitive only
option_c: DON'T SINK always followed by WHOOP WHOOP PULL UP
option_d: DON'T SINK followed by WHOOP WHOOP PULL UP if the sink rate overshoots a second level
explanation: In Mode 3, if the aircraft loses altitude after takeoff or during a go-around before establishing a positive climb, the GPWS generates a repetitive 'DON'T SINK' aural warning.

question_text: A ground proximity warning system (GPWS), when mandatorily installed on board an aircraft, must in all cases generate :
option_a: at least one sound alarm to which a visual alarm can be added
option_b: a sound alarm or a visual alarm
option_d: a visual alarm to which a sound alarm can be
explanation: The regulations dictate that a GPWS must automatically generate a distinctive, continuous aural warning, which may be supplemented by a flashing visual warning light.

question_text: The operation of the GPWS (Ground Proximity Warning System) is governed by laws taking the aircraft height into account as well as :1- the descent rate2- the climb rate3- the aircraft configuration4- the selected engine rpmThe combination of correct statements is :
explanation: GPWS algorithms monitor height above ground (radio altitude) along with the rate of descent (1) and the aircraft's physical landing configuration (3).

question_text: If an aircraft is flying (with flaps and landing gear retracted) in proximity to terrain and its GPWS (Ground Proximity Warning System) get activated, because it is detecting that the aeroplane has an excessive rate of descent, the system provides the following aural warning signals :
option_a: ""SINK RATE, SINK RATE"" followed by ""WHOOP WHOOP PULL UP"" (twice)
option_b: ""DON'T SINK, DON'T SINK""
option_c: ""TERRAIN, TERRAIN"" followed by ""WHOOP WHOOP PULL UP"" (twice)
option_d: ""TOO LOW, TERRAIN"" (twice) followed by ""TOO LOW GEAR"" (twice)
explanation: In Mode 1 (excessive descent rate), the GPWS first warns the pilot with 'SINK RATE, SINK RATE'. If the descent rate remains high, it transitions to a high-priority 'WHOOP WHOOP PULL UP' alarm.

question_text: If the GPWS (Ground Proximity Warning System) activates, and alerts the pilot with an aural warning ""DON'T SINK"" (twice times), it is because :
option_a: during take-off or missed approach manoeuvre, the aircraft has started to loose altitude.
option_b: the aircraft experiences an unexpected proximity to the terrain, with landing gear retracted.
option_c: at too low altitude, the aircraft has an excessive rate of descent.
option_d: the aircraft experiences an unexpected proximity to terrain, without landing-flap selected.
explanation: Mode 3 of the GPWS detects altitude loss (a sink) after takeoff or a missed approach when the landing gear and flaps are not in the landing configuration.

question_text: A transport airplane is compelled to carry on board a Ground Proximity Warning System (GPWS). This system will warn the crew in case of :1 - keeping the altitude at a lower level than the one shown in the flight plan entered in the FMS.2 - dangerous ground proximity.3 - loss of altitude during take-off or missed approach.4 - wrong landing configuration.5 - descent below glidepath, within limits.The combination regrouping all the correct statements is :
explanation: The GPWS provides protection against dangerous terrain proximity (2), altitude loss after takeoff/missed approach (3), incorrect configuration landing attempts (4), and glideslope deviations (5).

question_text: The Ground Proximity Warning System (GPWS) is a system working according to a height span ranging from :
option_a: 50 ft to 2 500 ft
option_b: the ground to 1 000 ft
explanation: The GPWS monitors the flight path and terrain clearance within an envelope between 50 feet and 2,500 feet radio altitude.

question_text: The GPWS (Ground Proximity Warning System) releases a warning in the following cases :1- excessive rate of descent2- excessive ground proximity rate3- loss of altitude after take-off or go-around4- abnormal gear/flaps configuration5- excessive deviation under the glidepath6- abnormal airbrakes configurationThe combination regrouping all the correct statements is:
explanation: The five primary modes of the GPWS cover excessive descent rate (1), terrain closure rate (2), altitude loss after takeoff (3), unsafe landing gear/flap configuration (4), and glideslope deviation (5). Airbrakes (6) are not standard GPWS inputs.

question_text: The requirement to carry a GPWS (Ground Proximity Warning System) concerns aeroplanes which are, depending on their age, weight and passenger capacity :1- turboprop-powered2- piston-powered3- jet-poweredThe combination regrouping all the correct statements is :
explanation: Regulations mandate GPWS installation for turbine-engine (turboprop (1) and turbojet (3)) commercial aircraft exceeding certain weight and passenger limits.

question_text: A Ground Proximity Warning System (GPWS) generates automatically a distinct warning to the flight crew with aural and/or light warning signals in the case of:1- an excessive rate of descent with respect to terrain2- a dangerous proximity to the ground3- a loss of altitude following take-off or go-around4- an abnormal flight attitude5- an abnormal landing configuration6- an abnormal deviation below ILS glide slopeThe combination regrouping all the correct statements is:
explanation: The five standard GPWS modes trigger alerts for excessive descent rate (1), terrain closure rate (2), sink after takeoff (3), landing gear/flap configuration (5), and glideslope deviation (6).

question_text: The inputs to the GPWS (Ground Proximity Warning System), are:1- Air Data Computer - (Mach number and Vertical Speed) 2- Radio Altimeter3- NAV/ILS (Glide Slope)4- NAV/VOR5- Flap (position)6- Angle of Attack7- Landing Gear (position)The combination of correct statement is:
explanation: The GPWS computer aggregates inputs from the Air Data Computer (1), radio altimeter (2), glide slope receiver (3), wing flaps (5), and landing gear (7).

question_text: The TCAS (Traffic Collision Avoidance System) is a proximity alarm system which detects a ""traffic"" when the conflicting traffic is equipped with a :
option_a: serviceable SSR transponder
option_b: serviceable weather radar
explanation: TCAS can only detect and track adjacent aircraft if those targets are equipped with an active, operating secondary surveillance radar (SSR) transponder (Mode A/C or Mode S).

question_text: A ""TCAS II"" (Traffic Collision Avoidance System) provides:
option_a: the intruder relative position and possibly an indication of a collision avoidance manoeuvre within the vertical plane only.
option_b: a simple intruding airplane proximity warning.
option_c: the intruder relative position and possibly an indication of a collision avoidance manoeuvre within both the vertical and horizontal planes.
option_d: the intruder relative position and possibly an indication of a collision avoidance manoeuvre within the horizontal plane only.
explanation: TCAS II detects traffic positions and issues Traffic Advisories (TAs) as well as Resolution Advisories (RAs) that command vertical maneuvers (e.g., climb/descend) to resolve conflicts. It does not issue horizontal maneuvers.

question_text: Concerning the TCAS (Traffic Collision Avoidance System) :
option_a: No protection is available against aircraft not equipped with a serviceable SSR transponder
option_b: In one of the system modes, the warning : ""TOO LOW TERRAIN"" is generated
option_c: In one of the system modes, the warning : ""PULL UP"" is generated
option_d: Resolution Advisory (RA) must not be followed without obtaining clearance from ATC
explanation: Because TCAS relies on active transponder interrogations, it is blind to and cannot offer protection against non-transponder-equipped aircraft (non-cooperative targets).

question_text: The TCAS (Traffic Collision Avoidance System) gives avoidance resolutions :
option_a: only in the vertical plane
option_b: only in the horizontal plane
explanation: The collision avoidance algorithms of TCAS II generate Resolution Advisories (RAs) that command changes to vertical speed only.

question_text: In the event of a conflict, the TCAS (Traffic Collision Avoidance System) will give information such as :
option_a: climb/descent
option_b: turn left/turn right
explanation: Under TCAS II logic, the resolution commands (RAs) issued to the pilot are vertical steering commands, directing a climb, descent, or a restriction on vertical speed.

question_text: The principle of the TCAS (Traffic Collision Avoidance Systems) is based on the use of :
option_a: transponders fitted in the aircraft
option_b: airborne weather radar system
explanation: TCAS works by transmitting interrogations from the host aircraft and receiving and processing replies from transponders installed on surrounding aircraft.

question_text: The TCAS 1 (Traffic Collision Avoidance System) provides :1- traffic information2- horizontal resolution (RA: Resolution Advisory)3- vertical resolution (RA: Resolution Advisory)4- ground proximity warningThe combination regrouping all the correct statements is:
explanation: TCAS I is a basic system that only provides Traffic Advisories (TAs) to alert the pilot of nearby traffic (Statement 1). It does not provide any Resolution Advisories (RAs) in the vertical or horizontal planes.

question_text: The TCAS 2 (Traffic Collision Avoidance System) provides :1- traffic information (TA: Traffic Advisory)2- horizontal resolution (RA: Resolution Advisory)3- vertical resolution (RA: Resolution Advisory)4- ground proximity warningThe combination regrouping all the correct statements is:
explanation: TCAS II provides both Traffic Advisories (TAs) to display traffic positions (1) and vertical Resolution Advisories (RAs) to command avoidance maneuvers (3).

question_text: The TCAS (Traffic Collision Avoidance System) computer receives information :1- about the pressure altitude through the mode S transponder2- from the radio- altimeter3- specific to the airplane configuration4- from the inertial unitsThe combination regrouping all the correct statements is:
explanation: The TCAS computer requires target altitude from the transponder (1), height above ground from the radio altimeter (2) to suppress RAs close to the ground, and aircraft-specific performance limits (3).

question_text: When the intruding aircraft is equipped with a transponder without altitude reporting capability, the TCAS (Traffic Collision Avoidance System) issues a :
option_a: ""traffic advisory"" only.
option_b: ""traffic advisory"" and vertical ""resolution advisory"".
explanation: If an intruding aircraft has a transponder without Mode C altitude reporting (Mode A only), TCAS can only determine range and bearing, and thus can only issue a Traffic Advisory (TA).

question_text: When the intruding aircraft is equipped with a serviceable mode C transponder, the TCAS II (Traffic Collision Avoidance System) generates a :
option_a: ""traffic advisory"" and vertical ""resolution advisory"".
option_b: ""traffic advisory"" and horizontal ""resolution advisory"".
explanation: If the intruder is equipped with a functioning Mode C (or Mode S) transponder, TCAS II receives altitude data and can issue both Traffic Advisories (TAs) and vertical Resolution Advisories (RAs).

question_text: On a TCAS2 (Traffic Collision Avoidance System), a corrective ""resolution advisory"" (RA) is a ""resolution advisory"":
option_a: asking the pilot to modify effectively the vertical speed of his aircraft.
option_b: which does not require any action from the pilot but on the contrary asks him not to modify his current vertical speed rate.
option_c: asking the pilot to modify the heading of his aircraft.
option_d: asking the pilot to modify the speed of his aircraft.
explanation: A corrective Resolution Advisory (RA) instructs the pilot to change their flight path by altering their vertical speed (e.g., 'Climb, Climb' when in level flight) to clear the traffic.

question_text: On a TCAS 2 (Traffic Collision Avoidance System) the preventive ""resolution advisory"" (RA) is a ""resolution advisory"":
option_a: that advises the pilot to avoid certain deviations from the current vertical rate but does not require any change to be made to that rate.
option_b: asking the pilot to modify effectively the vertical speed of his aircraft.
option_c: asking the pilot to modify the heading of his aircraft.
option_d: asking the pilot to modify the speed of his aircraft.
explanation: A preventive Resolution Advisory (RA) directs the pilot to maintain their current vertical speed and avoid certain vertical rates (e.g., 'Monitor Vertical Speed' or 'Do Not Climb').

question_text: An ""intruding traffic advisory"" is represented on the display system of the TCAS 2 (Traffic Collision Avoidance System) by displaying :
option_a: a yellow full circle.
option_b: a blue or white empty lozenge.
option_c: a blue or white full lozenge.
explanation: On the traffic display, a Traffic Advisory (TA) target is represented by a solid yellow circle.

question_text: A ""resolution advisory"" (RA) is represented on the display system of the TCAS 2 (Traffic Collision Avoidance System) by a :
option_a: red full square.
option_b: blue or white full lozenge.
explanation: A Resolution Advisory (RA) target is represented on the TCAS display by a solid red square, indicating an immediate threat.

question_text: A ""close traffic advisory"" is displayed on the display device of the TCAS 2 (Traffic Collision Avoidance System) by :
option_a: a blue or white empty lozenge.
option_b: an orange full circle.
option_c: a blue or white full lozenge.
explanation: Proximate traffic (traffic within 6 NM and +/- 1200 ft but not triggering a TA or RA) is represented by a solid blue or white diamond (lozenge).

question_text: The TCAS II data display devices can be in the form of:1- a specific dedicated screen 2- a screen combined with the weather radar3- a variometer represented on a liquid crystal screen which allows the display of Traffic Advisory (TA) and Resolution Advisory (RA)4- an EFIS (Electronic Flight Instrument System) screenThe combination regrouping all the correct statements is:
explanation: TCAS data can be displayed on a dedicated screen (1), integrated into the weather radar screen (2), shown as speed-restriction arcs on a digital VSI (3), or integrated into an EFIS navigation display (4).

question_text: The stick shaker calculator receives the following informations :1- mass of the airplane2- angle of attack3- wing flap deflection4- position of the landing gear5- total air temperature6- pressure altitudeThe combination regrouping all the correct statements is:
explanation: The stick shaker computer activates based on aerodynamic stall margins, calculating limits primarily using angle of attack (2) and wing flap deflection (3) to determine the aircraft configuration.

question_text: In some configurations, modern aircraft do not respect the regulatory margins between stall and natural buffet.The warning system supplies the corresponding alarm. The required margin related to the stall speed is:
explanation: Under EASA CS-25 certification regulations, the stall warning system must be activated to provide a margin of at least 7% (or 5 knots, whichever is greater) above the actual stalling speed.

question_text: The stall warning system receives information about the :1- airplane angle of attack2- airplane speed3- airplane bank angle4- airplane configuration5- load factor on the airplaneThe combination regrouping all the correct statements is:
explanation: The stall warning system determines the stall angle of attack limit based on the measured aerodynamic angle of attack (1) and the aircraft configuration (slat/flap position) (4).

question_text: A stall warning system is based on a measure of :
option_a: aerodynamic incidence.
option_b: airspeed.
explanation: Stall warning systems are based on the measurement of aerodynamic incidence (angle of attack), as a wing always stalls at a specific critical angle of attack regardless of weight or airspeed.

question_text: The main input data to the Stall Warning Annunciator System are :1- Mach Meter indication2- Angle of Attack3- Indicate Airspeed (IAS)4- Aircraft configuration (Flaps/Slats)The combination regrouping all the correct statements is :
explanation: The core inputs to compute stall margins are the measured angle of attack (aerodynamic incidence) (2) and the current flap and slat configuration (4).

question_text: The calculator combined with the stick shaker system of a modern transport airplane receives information about the: 1- angle of attack2- engine R.P.M.3- configuration4- pitch and bank attitude5- sideslipThe combination regrouping all the correct statements is:
option_a: 1 and 3.
explanation: The stick shaker activation threshold is computed as a function of the measured angle of attack (1) and the aircraft configuration (flap/slat position) (3).

question_text: The angle of attack transmitter provides an electric signal varying with:1- the angular position of a wind vane2- the deviation between the airplane flight attitude and the path calculated by the inertial unit3- a probe differential pressure depending on the variation of the angle of attackThe combination regrouping all the correct statements is:
option_a: 1 and 3.
explanation: An angle of attack sensor measures local airflow angle by tracking the physical deflection of a wind vane (1) or by detecting the differential pressure across ports on a slotted probe (3).

question_text: The angle of attack transmitters placed laterally on the forward part of the fuselage supply an electrical signal indicating:1- the angular position of a wind vane2- a differential pressure in a probe, depending on the variation of the angle of attack3- a differential pressure in a probe, depending on the variation of the speedThe combination regrouping all the correct statements is:
explanation: Fuselage-mounted angle of attack transmitters supply electrical outputs proportional to the angular position of a wind vane (1) or the differential pressure across slots in a probe (2).

question_text: The oncoming stall of a large transport airplane appears in the form of:
option_a: control stick vibrations simulating natural buffeting.
option_b: an orange light on the warning display.
option_c: a natural buffeting which occurs prior to the simulated buffeting.
explanation: Large transport aircraft often lack clear natural aerodynamic buffeting prior to stall. A stick shaker is therefore installed to shake the control column, simulating natural buffet to warn the pilot.

question_text: The stall warning system of a large transport airplane includes:1- an angle of attack sensor 2- a computer3- a transmitter originating from the anemometer4- an independent pitot probe5- a transmitter of the flap/slat position indicating systemThe combination regrouping all the correct statements is:
explanation: A stall warning system consists of an angle of attack sensor (1), a computer to calculate the stall threshold (2), and flap/slat position transmitters (5) to determine configuration.

question_text: Flight recorder duration must be such that flight data, cockpit voice and sound warnings may respectively be recorded during at least:
option_a: 25 hours for flight data, 30 minutes for cockpit voices and warnings horns.
option_b: 24 hours for flight data, 60 minutes for cockpit voices and warnings horns.
option_c: 20 hours for flight data, 15 minutes for cockpit voices and warnings horns.
option_d: 48 hours for flight data, 60 minutes for cockpit voices and warnings horns
explanation: Under standard aviation regulations, the Flight Data Recorder (FDR) must retain at least the last 25 hours of flight data, while the Cockpit Voice Recorder (CVR) must record at least the last 30 minutes of cockpit communications and ambient sounds.

question_text: The flight data recorder must start data recording automatically:
option_a: before the airplane is able to move by under its own power.
option_b: when taking-off.
option_c: when the landing gear is retracted.
explanation: The Flight Data Recorder (FDR) must start recording automatically before the aircraft begins taxiing under its own power (e.g., when engines are started or parking brake is released) to ensure all taxi and takeoff parameters are recorded.

question_text: The flight data recorder must automatically stop data recording when the:
option_a: airplane cannot any longer move by its own power.
option_b: main gear shock strut compresses when touching the runway.
option_c: landing gear is extended and locked.
explanation: The FDR is configured to automatically stop recording only after the aircraft has come to a complete stop and the engines are shut down (cannot move under its own power).

question_text: In accordance with (ICAO) Annex 6 part I, the flight data recorder is to be located in the aircraft :
option_a: as far to the rear as practicable
option_b: as far forward as practicable
option_c: as near to the landing gear as practicable
option_d: at the right or left wing tip
explanation: Under ICAO Annex 6 standards, the FDR and CVR must be installed in the aft section of the fuselage (as far to the rear as practicable) to maximize survivability in a crash, as the rear fuselage suffers the lowest impact forces.

question_text: Except for airplanes under 5,7 t airworthiness certificate of which is subsequent to 31 march 1998, a flight data recording system must be able to store the recorded data for a minimum of the last :
option_a: 25 hours.
option_b: 10 hours.
explanation: Except for smaller or older categories, standard digital flight data recorders (DFDRs) must be capable of storing at least the last 25 hours of recorded flight parameter data.

question_text: The CVR (Cockpit Voice Recorder) includes:1. a microphone2. a recorder in compliance with the shock and fire resistance standards3. an independent battery4. a flight data recorderThe combination regrouping all the correct statements is:
explanation: The CVR system includes cockpit microphones (1) to capture voice and ambient sounds, and the highly protected recording unit (2) designed to survive high impact, water immersion, and fire.

question_text: The flight data recorders must preserve the conversation and aural warnings of the last :
option_a: 30 minutes of operation
option_b: 25 hours of operation
explanation: Older or standard CVR requirements mandate that the voice recording must preserve the last 30 minutes of cockpit conversations, aural warnings, and radio communications (though modern regulations are extending this to 2 hours or more).

question_text: According to the JAR-OPS regulations, the Cockpit Voice Recorder of a 50 seat multi-engined aircraft having been granted the airworthiness certificate after 1st April 1998 will record:1- the radiotelephonic communications transmitted or received by the cockpit crew2- the audio environment of the cockpit3- the cabin attendants communications in the cabin via the interphone4- the flight crew members communications in the cockpit via the interphone5- the flight crew members communications in the cockpit via the public address system6- the audio signals identifiying the navigation or approach aidsThe combination regrouping the correct statements is:
explanation: The CVR is designed to record radio communications (1), cockpit background noise (2), flight deck interphone conversations (4), public address announcements (5), and navigation aid identification tones (6).

question_text: According to the JAR-OPS regulations, the Cockpit Voice Recorder of a 50 seat multi-engined aircraft, having been granted an airworthiness certificate after 1st April 1998, shall start recording :
option_a: Automatically prior to the aircraft moving under its own power until flight completion when the aircraft is no longer able to move under its own power.
option_b: Automatically when the wheels leave the ground until the moment when the wheels touch the ground again.
option_c: From the first radio contact with Air Traffic Control until radio shutdown after the flight.
option_d: When the pilot selects the ""CVR: ON"" during engine start until the pilot selects the ""CVR: OFF"" during the engine shut down.
explanation: The CVR must start recording automatically before the aircraft moves under its own power and continue recording until the flight is complete and the engines are shut down.
